translation:
_Main Ayodhyamein jeevana, man mero Gokul manhi |_
_Rishi patni su kol hai, ve birad bisarat naahi ||_
(Though I dwell in Ayodhya, my mind remains in Gokul; the vow given to the sages' wives - that pledge is never forgotten.)

In the Dwapar Yuga, when Lord Shri Krishna used to go into the forest to graze the cows, he was accompanied by companion cowherds of his own age. The Bhagavatam gives their number as sixteen. These sixteen child-companions of Krishna grazed the cows in the forest and performed many kinds of divine plays (leelas). The Puranas tell how, during Rama's life, while in exile in the forest Rama served the sages a great deal, but he did not, in particular, accept any service from the sages themselves or from their wives. Because of this, the sages' wives said to Rama, "Grant us too the good fortune of serving you." Rama then promised them that in the Dwapar Yuga their wish would be fulfilled. And here, they have all come in the form of the gopis and perform their divine play in Gokul. The story of all these gopas and gopis is well known.

Among the sixteen companions in Gokul, one who remained constantly in Krishna's service was, in this present birth, Kabirji; the second was Jivanji Maharaj; the third was Narsinh Mehta. All of them remained ever absorbed in the service of Krishna. Today, at the place called Bansivat in Vrindavan - where the Lord once performed the rasleela (divine dance-play) - there stands, in the form of a marble statue, a depiction of the playful sport (chhakleela) of these sixteen child-companions. The image of Jivanji Maharaj that we see today has been copied from there; beside him Kabirji is seated. These images have been placed there upon a raised platform, and the Tourism Department of the Government of India has given a certificate here declaring this to be the original Bansivat.
